source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἅπαξ εἰς τὸν περὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἤλθομεν λόγον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν, τοῖς πιστεύουσι θείῳ πνεύματι αὐτοὺς λελαληκέναι, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἔσται ἀχρήσιμα τὰ ἐποισθησόμενα (ἀλλὰ) καὶ τοῖς εὐγνωμονοῦσι δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον παραδέξασθαι ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι προφήτας εἶχον, εἴπερ ἔμελλον συνέχεσθαι ἐν τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς νομοθεσίᾳ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, καθάπερ εἰλήφεισαν, καὶ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἔχειν ἀφορμὰς ἀποστῆναι εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν πολυθεότητα. τὸ δ᾿ ἀναγκαῖον οὕτω παραστήσομεν. „τὰ ἔθνη,“ ὡς γέγραπται καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νόμῳ, „κληδόνων καὶ μαντειῶν ἀκούσονται“· τῷ δὲ λαῷ ἐκείνῳ εἴρηται· „σοὶ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔδωκε κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ καὶ ἐπιφέρεται τούτῳ τὸ „προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ εἴπερ οὖν τῶν ἐθνῶν χρωμένων μαντείαις εἴτε διὰ „κληδόνων“ εἴτε δι᾿ οἰωνῶν εἴτε δι᾿ ὀρνίθων εἴτε δι᾿ ἐγγαστριμύθων εἴτε καὶ διὰ τῶν τὴν θυτικὴν ἐπαγγελλομένων εἴτε καὶ διὰ Χαλδαίων γενεθλιαλογούντων, ἅπερ πάντα Ἰουδαίοις ἀπείρητο. Ἰουδαῖοι εἰ μηδεμίαν εἶχον παραμυθίαν γνώσεως τῶν μελλόντων, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἂν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὴν γνῶσιν λιχνείας τῶν ἐσομένων ἀγόμενοι κατεφρόνησαν μὲν ἂν τῶν ἰδίων ὡς οὐδὲν ἐχόντων θεῖον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ οὐκ ἂν μετὰ Μω(??)σέα προφήτην προσήκαντο οὐδ᾿ ἀνέγραψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς λόγους, αὐτόμολοι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν μαντεῖα καὶ χρηστήρια μετέστησαν ἢ ἐπεχείρησαν ἂν ἱδρῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον καὶ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς. ὥστ᾿ οὐδὲν ἄτοπόν ἐστι καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τοὺς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς προφήτας εἰς παραμυθίαν τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποθούντων προειρηκέναι, ὥστε καὶ „περὶ ὄνων ἀπολωλυιῶν“ προφητεύειν τὸν Σαμουὴλ καὶ περὶ νόσου παιδὸς βασιλικοῦ τὸν ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἀναγεγραμμένον. πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων μαντείαν λαβεῖν ἐπέπλησσον οἱ τὰ τοῦ νόμου Ἰουδαίων πρεσβεύοντες; ὥσπερ εὑρίσκεται Ἠλίας τῷ Ὀχοζίᾳ ἐπιπλήσσων καὶ λέγων· „εἰ παρὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι θεὸν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ὑμεῖς πορεύεσθε ἐκζητῆσαι ἐν τῇ Βαὰλ μυῖαν θεὸν Ἀκκαρῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Since we have once come to the discourse about the prophets, for the Jews, who believe that they spoke by the divine Spirit, the things that will be said will not be useless, but also for the Greeks who are well-disposed. To whom we will say that it is necessary to accept that the Jews also had prophets, if indeed they were going to persist in the law given to them and believe in the Creator, just as they had received, and not have a starting point to revolt to the polytheism of the nations. We will present the necessary thing in this way. 'The nations', as it is written also in the law of the Jews, 'will listen to soothsayers and diviners'; but to that people it has been said: 'The Lord your God has not given this to you.' And it is added to this: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers.' If, then, the nations use divination, either through 'soothsayers' or through birds or through entrails or through ventriloquists or through those who promise sacrifices or through Chaldeans who calculate nativities, all of which were forbidden to the Jews, the Jews would not have had any consolation of knowledge of future things, they would have been led by the same human curiosity about knowledge of future things, they would have despised their own as having nothing divine in themselves, and they would not have added a prophet after Moses, nor would they have written down their words, but they would have deserted to the divinations and oracles of the nations or would have tried to establish something of this kind among themselves. So it is not at all absurd that the prophets among them spoke for the consolation of those who long for such things, so that even Samuel prophesied about donkeys that had been lost and the one written in the third book of Kings about the illness of the king's child. How would the Jewish elders, who preside over the law, have rebuked someone who wanted to take divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ochozias and saying: 'If it is not that there is no God in Israel, you go to seek in the fly god of Ekron.'

choices.why: describes the attitude of the Greeks

pass_b_english: Now that we have turned to the subject of the prophets, what follows will prove useful not only for Jews, who hold that the prophets spoke by the divine Spirit, but also for well-disposed Greeks. We will tell these readers that they must accept that the Jews possessed prophets as well. Otherwise, the Jews could not have continued in the law given to them, maintained their faith in the Creator as they had received it, or resisted any impulse to abandon their heritage for the polytheism of the nations. We will demonstrate this necessity as follows. Scripture says, 'The nations will listen to soothsayers and diviners' (Deuteronomy 18:14). Yet to Israel God declared, 'The Lord your God has not given this to you' (Deuteronomy 18:14). He adds, 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers' (Deuteronomy 18:15). Now the nations practice divination through soothsayers, the flight of birds, the reading of entrails, ventriloquists, those who promise sacrificial rites, and Chaldean astrologers who cast nativities—all of which were forbidden to the Jews. If the Jews had lacked any divinely given consolation for knowing the future, mere human curiosity about what is to come would have driven them to despise their own institutions as devoid of the divine. They would never have accepted another prophet after Moses, nor preserved the prophets' words. Instead, they would have defected to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or attempted to establish such practices among themselves. Therefore, it is not at all absurd that their prophets spoke beforehand to comfort those who long for such knowledge—so that even Samuel prophesied about lost donkeys, and the prophet recorded in the third book of Kings spoke concerning the illness of a royal child (2 Kings 1:2-3). How else would the Jewish elders who administer the law have rebuked anyone who sought divination from idols? Just as Elijah rebuked Ahaziah: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?' (2 Kings 1:3).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional structure of the Greek text (the 'if... they would have...' construction regarding the Jews' lack of prophecy). Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required inline scripture citations (Deuteronomy 18:14, 18:15, 2 Kings 1:2-3) which were alluded to in the Greek but not explicitly numbered. The translation of 'Βαὰλ μυῖαν' as 'Baal-zebub' (or 'fly god') and 'Ἀκκαρῶν' as 'Ekron' is appropriate for the context of the Elijah narrative.
